moves.spoken: We take the white pieces and steer for the Glek System.
Black's knight comes to f6 and we answer with the knight to c3, heading into the Four Knights.
We fianchetto with g3 — the move that defines the Glek.
Black chooses the bishop to e7.
Black plays d6 — a modest, passive setup: nothing outright wrong with it, but it lets us do whatever we like.
The more testing tries in the Glek are the bishop to c5, the bishop to b4, and the ...d5 break — Black's three main lines; this bishop-e7 setup is the passive cousin.
We castle.

Black develops the bishop to e6, which tempts d4 — but in the Glek be careful with that push. Not because Black might trade everything on d4 (that suits us fine), but because of ...Bg4: even at the cost of a tempo it hangs the d4-pawn and can force us to close with d5, betraying the whole spirit of the system. Ducking it by taking on e5 is a dull move that invites mass exchanges.
So instead of an immediate d4 we play h3, keeping our options open and preparing d4 under better circumstances (the quiet d3 is also available).
Black replies h6 — and now d4 will work.
We push d4. It works like a charm: it threatens a fork and all but forces Black to release the tension.
Black captures on d4 and we recapture with the knight.
The knights come off on d4 and our queen recaptures, landing us a very pleasant position — but we mustn't forget the h3-pawn.
Black centralizes the queen to d7.
We step the king to h2 to defend h3. Careful here: many players castle queenside instead and simply hang the a7-pawn — a mistake I've seen again and again.

Black lunges h5, trying for a kingside attack — but knowing the system, you see it isn't one: Black threatens nothing. To ...h4 we simply push g4, and a sac like ...Bxg4 is futile — the position is too passive, there aren't enough attackers, and our king is far too safe.
Notice the bishop on e6 has run out of squares — so f4 comes naturally, grabbing space and setting a very nasty threat.
Black plays c5. And yes, White's plan is genuinely hard to meet: as long as we deny the bishop its escape, f5 is a monstrous threat.
That tells us where the queen belongs — d3, guarding the c4-square and discouraging ...b5 (which wasn't dangerous anyway, since e5 would answer it).
Black plays g6 — but it doesn't stop f5.
We play f5. The game is effectively over — after the coming exchanges the e6-bishop is trapped.
Black takes with the g-pawn on f5.
We recapture with the e-pawn on f5 — the bishop is trapped and our position fully open.
Black tries c4, but it changes nothing. We could lift the queen to f3, but simpler is to capture on e6.
We take on e6, hitting the queen on d7.
Black recaptures on e6. Now reposition the queen toward f3 — but note, with the king on h2 under an x-ray, keep an eye on a sudden ...Ng4 check; in the right setting it can be very nasty.
Here the check would be harmless — our king just steps to g1 — but there's no reason to invite it. Instead the queen goes to f5, more to the point, and now the queen trade can't be avoided.
Black castles long. There's no reason for us to capture on e6 ourselves — it would only repair Black's pawns and help build a central chain.
So instead we play the bishop to g5, hitting the knight — this should win further material, since after a queen trade on f5 and the rook recapture the pin tells.
Black tries the knight to g4 with check, but we simply take it — the g1-square is free.
We capture on g4.
Black checks on g4 and we tuck the king to g1.
Black recaptures the bishop on g5.
We don't need the queen — we just take the bishop back on g5, staying up two minor pieces. Always watch the a7–g1 diagonal, but with no checks there our king is perfectly safe.
Black tucks the king to b8. We're up two pieces — time to bring a rook to the centre.
The rook swings to e1, heading for the seventh rank — and the capture on f7 is coming. It's over.
Black plays the queen to d7.
We plant the rook on e7.
Black's queen retreats to c8.
Simpler than taking on b7 is to double on f7.
Black pushes d5.
We take on b7 with check, winning the queen and mopping up everything loose.
The queens come off, we recapture with check, and the bishop check on d5 opens the hunt for the king.
A check on f6 herds the king forward.
The king walks to c5. Chasing the very fastest mate here is fiddly.
So don't agonize over the quickest path — just keep checking and the mate arrives. We check on c6.
The king steps to d4 and the knight checks from b5 — Black walks right into it.

The king goes to e5 and the queen delivers mate on e6. The takeaway on the Glek: you don't have to prevent ...Bg4 in general — if Black plays it, h3 and then g4 just shove the bishop to a passive square. It's ONLY when you intend d4 that stopping ...Bg4 matters, because d4 ...Bg4 forces the closed, King's-Indian-like structure you don't want from a Glek. If you'd rather not bother with h3 or d4 at all, the quiet d3 setup is fine — it just doesn't squeeze the most from the position. Against this passive setup White simply does everything he wants: fianchetto, seize the centre, and Black stays paralysed until he can free himself with ...d5.
